thag11.1:1.1: These two verses abound in obscurities and odd transitions, and both commentary and Norman have struggled with them. I think their style evokes the choppiness of people yelling over a wild storm, so I try to echo this in my rendering.
thag11.1:1.2: _Ujjuhāna_ is otherwise unknown. The commentary says it is either a mountain or a bird; the latter fits the imagery better, as the monk reminds the speaker of a bird in the rain. Perhaps it is the hoopoe, known for its crest that may be raised upright (_ujju_) or lowered (_hāna_) at will, and whose upper plumage is a monkish orange-brown.
thag11.1:1.3: Accept _verambha_ over the variant _veramba_ preferred by Norman, on the strength of [an3.35:2.1]() where it clearly refers to winds that are “raging” (_vi_ + _rambha_). _Vairambha_ winds are mentioned in Subala Upaniṣad 15 and Liṅga Purāṇa 86.87, seemingly in reference to bodily winds. This seems to be a statement in astonishment or perhaps sarcasm; “delightful” (_ramaṇīya_) is typically used for pleasant parks or lakes. There is no explicit question marker, but I take it as continuing the question that makes up the whole verse.
thag11.1:2.3: Here, “perceptions” are connected with seclusion, just as “recollection” is so connected at [an6.30:10.2](). It must mean “meditative perceptions”, such as the ten of [an10.60](). | _Abhikīrati_ (with _ī_ lengthened *metri causa*) elsewhere means “engulf” ([dhp25:4](), [sn2.18:2.4]()), but here _abhikirati_ parallels _nudati_ (“disperse”). It is a transitive verb, but the poet has elected to omit the object. The sense is, “My meditations, being connected with seclusion, dispel (the clouds of the mind).”
thag11.1:3.1: Again the poet chooses obscurity. He sees a crow that reminds him of the charnel ground, the inevitable destiny of his own body. But he chooses not to name the animal, instead describing through paradox—though born of the white egg, it has no white in it, just as life born in hope must end in death.
thag11.1:4.3: The parallel to this verse at [ja10]() is identical except it is addressed to a king. The form there is unambiguously vocative (_rāja_), so I take _bhikkhu_ here as also vocative, although the commentary reads it as nominative. | These verses are linked in two respects with [an3.35](): comfort in the midst of “raging” winds, and sleeping at ease.
thag11.1:5.2: _Gonaṅgula_ (“cow-tailed one”) is said by both the Pali commentary and Sanskrit (_golāṅgūla_) sources to mean a black monkey with a tail like a cow; several sources, however, specify the distinctive black face of the common grey langur.
